title: Polarization
idea: A radio wave is an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles. Polarization is the direction the electric field points.

items: Electric and magnetic fields, at right angles
The orientation of the electric field
Long-distance CW and SSB on VHF/UHF

config.heading: Line up the antennas
config.lead: Pick the path, then set each antenna.

situations.label: Line of sight on VHF or UHF
situations.title: Line of sight

rules.title: Matched: full strength
rules.text: Both electric fields point the same way, so the signal comes through at full strength.

rules.title: Matched: full strength
rules.text: Both electric fields point the same way, so the signal comes through at full strength.

rules.title: Cross-polarized: weaker
rules.text: One antenna is vertical and the other horizontal, so received signal strength is reduced.

rules.title: Cross-polarized: weaker
rules.text: One antenna is vertical and the other horizontal, so received signal strength is reduced.

situations.label: Bounced off the ionosphere
situations.title: Either antenna works
situations.text: Signals come back from the ionosphere elliptically polarized, so vertical or horizontal antennas both work for sending and receiving.

situations.label: Long-distance CW and SSB on VHF or UHF
situations.title: Use horizontal
situations.text: Horizontal polarization is normal for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on VHF and UHF.

compare.how: At right angles to the electric field. Not what defines polarization.

traps.wrong: The orientation of the magnetic field
traps.why: Close, but polarization is set by the electric field.

traps.wrong: By the orientation of the magnetic field
traps.why: Antenna polarization is the orientation of the electric field.
The two fields are at right angles to each other.
Vertical is for FM and repeaters. Long-distance CW and SSB on VHF/UHF use horizontal.
Cross-polarized antennas on a line-of-sight path give a weaker received signal.

traps.wrong: Both the transmitting and receiving antennas must be of the same polarization
traps.why: Ionospheric signals are elliptically polarized, so either antenna works.
A radio wave's two parts are the electric and magnetic fields.
